well-taboo-sexual-health.title: Adult sexual health, deeper: methods, infections, desire & every life stage
well-taboo-sexual-health.description: Goes beyond the basics in well-reproductive and wellbeing-sexuality-education: contraception compared in detail, emergency contraception, STIs and the HPV vaccine, consent in long relationships, sexual difficulties, myths, and sex after childbirth and after 50. Adults only (18+). General education, not medical or legal advice.

courses.title: Contraception compared: choosing what fits your life
courses.summary: A side-by-side look at every common method available in India — how it works, typical-use effectiveness, side effects, who should avoid it and how to switch.
outcomes: Compare methods by typical-use failure rate
Explain how hormonal and non-hormonal methods work
Identify medical reasons to avoid some methods
Plan a conversation with a doctor about choosing or switching
courses.guardianNote: Adults-only (18+) course: medically accurate, non-explicit and judgment-free health education.

scenes.text: Ritu, 26, has used the pill for two years but keeps forgetting doses on night shifts.
Aman says condoms are '98% safe' so they should be fine.
Their doctor explains why real-life numbers differ from box numbers.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Two kinds of numbers
steps.body: **Perfect use** = failure rate when a method is used exactly right every time. **Typical use** = what happens in real life, including forgotten pills and condoms put on late. Typical use is the number that matters for planning.

steps.title: Approximate typical-use pregnancies per 100 users in a year (WHO/CDC-type figures)
steps.body:
- Implant: under 1
- Hormonal or copper IUD: under 1
- Sterilisation (vasectomy or tubal): under 1
- Injectable (e.g. DMPA, 'Antara' in the government programme): about 4
- Pill, patch, ring: about 7
- Male condom: about 13
- Withdrawal: about 20
- Female condom: about 21
- Fertility-awareness methods: roughly 2–23 depending on method and discipline

steps.title: The 'forgettable' principle
steps.body: Methods you do not have to remember (implant, IUD, sterilisation) are the most effective in real life because human error is removed.

steps.title: Only condoms protect against STIs
steps.body: No hormonal method, IUD or sterilisation protects against STIs or HIV. Many couples use condoms *plus* another method ('dual protection').

statements.s: A condom's typical-use failure is higher than its perfect-use failure.
statements.why: Late application, breakage and slipping all happen in real life.

statements.s: The pill protects against STIs.
statements.why: Only barrier methods (condoms) reduce STI risk.

statements.s: An IUD is among the most effective reversible methods.
statements.why: Under 1 pregnancy per 100 users per year.

statements.s: Withdrawal is as effective as the pill.
statements.why: Typical-use failure is about 20 per 100 versus about 7.

quiz.q: Which number best predicts real-life results?
quiz.why: Typical use includes ordinary human mistakes.

quiz.q: Which method is LEAST affected by user error?
quiz.why: Once inserted it works for years without daily action.

quiz.q: What is 'dual protection'?
quiz.why: Two condoms increase friction and breakage; condom + another method is the advice.

quiz.q: Roughly how many in 100 typical pill users become pregnant in a year?
quiz.why: Missed and late pills cause most failures.

lessons.title: How each method works and who should be careful

scenes.text: Meena, 34, gets migraines with aura and wants to start the combined pill.
Her doctor checks her blood pressure, smoking status and migraine history first.
They choose a copper IUD instead.

steps.title: Hormonal methods
steps.body: **Combined methods** (pill, patch, ring) contain oestrogen + progestogen and mainly stop ovulation. **Progestogen-only** methods (mini-pill, injectable, implant, hormonal IUD) thicken cervical mucus and may stop ovulation. India's public programme also offers **centchroman ('Chhaya')**, a non-steroidal weekly pill.

steps.title: Non-hormonal methods
steps.body: **Copper IUD**: copper is toxic to sperm; works for 5–10 years depending on type. **Condoms** (male/female): barrier. **Sterilisation**: vasectomy (blocks the vas deferens; a semen test is needed before relying on it) or tubal ligation — intended as permanent.

steps.title: Combined oestrogen methods are not for everyone
steps.body: Doctors avoid combined methods for people with migraine with aura, a past blood clot, some heart conditions, smokers over 35, and in the first weeks after childbirth. Progestogen-only or copper methods are often options instead.

steps.title: Common, usually harmless side effects
steps.body: Irregular spotting (implant, injectable, mini-pill), heavier periods (copper IUD), breast tenderness or nausea early on (combined pill). Many settle in 3 months. Fertility returns quickly after most methods; after the injectable it can take several months.

steps.title: Switching
steps.body: Switch with your doctor's guidance so there is no gap in protection — many switches are 'start the new method before stopping the old'.

activity.prompt: Sort each method by how it mainly works

quiz.q: Why is the combined pill often avoided in migraine with aura?
quiz.why: Oestrogen plus aura migraine raises stroke risk.

quiz.q: How does a copper IUD work?
options: Copper is toxic to sperm and eggs

quiz.q: After a vasectomy, a couple should…
options: Use other contraception until a semen test confirms no sperm
quiz.why: Sperm can remain in the tubes for weeks.

quiz.q: Which method may delay return of fertility for several months?
quiz.why: Return of fertility after DMPA can take months.

scenes.text: Kabir's cousin forwards: 'IUDs cause infertility and pills cause cancer.'
Kabir and his wife Sana nearly stop all contraception.
A family doctor walks them through the evidence.

steps.title: Myth: the pill makes you infertile
steps.body: False. Fertility returns soon after stopping the pill — often within the next cycle.

steps.title: Myth: an IUD causes abortion or infertility
steps.body: False. IUDs prevent fertilisation; they are not abortion. Fertility returns after removal. A small infection risk exists around insertion, which is why STI screening is offered when needed.

steps.title: Myth: you can't get pregnant during your period or the first time
steps.body: False. Sperm can survive up to about 5 days, and cycles vary. The first time carries the same risk as any other time.

steps.title: The pill and cancer
steps.body: Combined pill use is linked with *lower* lifetime risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer and a small, temporary rise in breast-cancer risk while using it. Discuss your personal history with a doctor.

steps.title: Check sources
steps.body: Prefer your doctor, a government health centre, or WHO/ICMR material over forwards and social media.

statements.s: You can't get pregnant the first time.
statements.why: Any unprotected sex can cause pregnancy.

statements.s: An IUD causes infertility.
statements.why: Fertility returns after removal.

statements.s: Sperm can survive several days in the reproductive tract.
statements.why: Up to about 5 days.

statements.s: The combined pill is associated with lower ovarian cancer risk.
statements.why: This protective effect is well documented.

quiz.q: Fertility after stopping the pill usually returns…
options: Quickly, often within a cycle or two
quiz.why: The pill does not cause infertility.

quiz.q: An IUD works mainly by…
Can pregnancy happen from sex during a period?
quiz.why: Sperm survival and short cycles make it possible.

quiz.q: Best source for contraception decisions?
options: A doctor or government health centre

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — help a couple choose a method

story.title: Shalini and Joseph plan their next five years

scenes.text: Shalini, 30, had a baby 4 months ago and is breastfeeding.
Joseph wants something 'that doesn't bother her'.
They visit the PHC to choose.

steps.title: Think like a counsellor
steps.body: Ask: How soon do you want a child (if ever)? Any medical conditions? Are you breastfeeding? Do you want hormones or not? Do you need STI protection?

steps.title: After childbirth
steps.body: Combined oestrogen methods are usually avoided in the early postpartum weeks and while exclusively breastfeeding; progestogen-only methods, copper IUD (often inserted soon after delivery or after 4–6 weeks) and condoms are common choices.

steps.title: Shared decision
steps.body: The person whose body the method is in has the final say. A partner's role is support, cost-sharing and remembering condoms or considering vasectomy.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body:
- **112** — any emergency
- **Tele-MANAS 14416** — free 24×7 mental health support
- A registered doctor, gynaecologist, urologist, psychiatrist or counsellor for anything personal

This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

a.text: The nurse asks what matters most to them. Shalini says: 'No daily pills, I'm too tired.' What do you suggest they discuss?

choices.label: Long-acting options like a copper IUD or implant
choices.feedback: Good — no daily action and safe with breastfeeding.

choices.label: The combined pill
choices.feedback: Daily, and oestrogen is usually avoided early postpartum while breastfeeding.

choices.label: Withdrawal, it's free
choices.feedback: About 20 in 100 typical-use failure — poor fit for 'no surprises'.

b.text: Joseph asks if he could share the responsibility. What's a respectful answer?

choices.label: Yes — condoms, and if they're sure they want no more children, vasectomy is a simple procedure
choices.feedback: Vasectomy is quicker and lower-risk than tubal sterilisation.

choices.label: No, contraception is a woman's job
choices.feedback: Responsibility can be shared.

end.text: They leave with a plan and a follow-up date. Choosing together, with accurate facts, is what good care looks like.

quiz.why: Oestrogen can affect milk supply and clot risk is raised postpartum.

courses.title: Emergency contraception, STIs & the HPV vaccine
courses.summary: What to do in the days after unprotected sex, how common STIs show up (or don't), how testing works, treatment, PEP for HIV, and why the HPV vaccine matters.
outcomes: Explain emergency contraception options and time windows
Recognise that many STIs have no symptoms
Describe when and how to test
Know about PEP, PrEP and the HPV vaccine
courses.guardianNote: Adults-only (18+) course: medically accurate, non-explicit and judgment-free health education.

scenes.text: Neha and Rahul's condom broke on Saturday night.
On Sunday morning Neha goes to a pharmacy.
The pharmacist explains her options calmly.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Options
steps.body:
- **Levonorgestrel EC pill**: a single-dose tablet sold at pharmacies; licensed for use up to 72 hours (3 days); works best the sooner it is taken.
- **Copper IUD** inserted by a clinician within 5 days: the most effective emergency method, and it then continues as contraception.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: EC pills mainly delay or prevent ovulation. They do **not** end an established pregnancy and are not abortion pills.

steps.title: Not for regular use
steps.body: EC is a backup, not a routine method — it is less effective than regular contraception. Repeated use is not dangerous but is unreliable.

steps.title: After EC
steps.body: The next period may be a few days early or late. Take a pregnancy test if the period is more than 7 days late, or very light. Consider an STI test if the risk applies.

statements.s: EC pills work better the sooner they are taken.
statements.why: Effectiveness drops with time.

statements.s: EC pills cause abortion.
statements.why: They act before pregnancy is established.

statements.s: A copper IUD can be used as emergency contraception.
statements.why: Within 5 days; most effective EC.

statements.s: EC protects against STIs.
statements.why: It does nothing against infections.

quiz.q: Most effective emergency contraception?
quiz.why: Copper IUD is the most effective EC.

quiz.q: Levonorgestrel EC is licensed for use up to…
What do EC pills mainly do?
When should you take a pregnancy test after EC?
options: If the period is more than about 7 days late

lessons.title: STIs: the silent ones and the noticeable ones

scenes.text: Vikram, 29, feels fine but his new partner asks him to get tested.
'I'd know if I had something,' he says.
His test shows chlamydia — with zero symptoms.

steps.title: Often no symptoms
steps.body: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea (especially in women), HPV, early HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis can be silent. That is why testing, not feeling, tells you your status.

steps.title: Possible symptoms
steps.body: Unusual discharge, burning when passing urine, sores or blisters, warts, pelvic pain, pain during sex, rashes, swollen glands. Any of these deserves a clinic visit.

steps.title: Treatable vs manageable
steps.body: **Curable** with the right antibiotics: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, trichomoniasis. **Manageable** with medicines: herpes, HIV (modern treatment lets people live long, healthy lives; with an undetectable viral load HIV is not transmitted sexually — 'U=U'), hepatitis B. Partners also need treatment to avoid re-infection.

steps.title: Untreated infections
steps.body: Untreated chlamydia/gonorrhoea can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility. Syphilis in pregnancy can harm the baby — which is why antenatal screening is routine.

activity.prompt: Sort: curable with antibiotics, or manageable long-term?

quiz.q: How do you know your STI status?
Which is curable with antibiotics?
What does U=U mean?
quiz.why: Effective HIV treatment prevents sexual transmission.

quiz.q: Why must partners be treated too?

lessons.title: Testing, PEP, PrEP and the HPV vaccine

scenes.text: Farah, 24, is nervous about going to an STI clinic.
She finds a government ICTC (Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre) where HIV testing is free and confidential.
The counsellor is kind; it takes under an hour.

steps.title: Where to test
steps.body: Government ICTCs and 'Suraksha' STI clinics offer free, confidential testing; private labs and gynaecologists/dermato-venereologists also test. National AIDS helpline: **1097**.

steps.title: Window periods
steps.body: Tests need time after exposure to detect infection. Modern HIV combination tests detect most infections by about 6 weeks; a negative test soon after a risk is often repeated later, as advised by the clinic.

steps.title: PEP and PrEP
steps.body: **PEP** (post-exposure prophylaxis) is a 28-day course of HIV medicines started as soon as possible and within **72 hours** after a possible exposure — go to a hospital or ART centre urgently. **PrEP** is taken before possible exposure by people at ongoing higher risk, under medical supervision.

steps.title: HPV vaccine
steps.body: HPV causes almost all cervical cancer and some throat, anal and penile cancers. Vaccination works best before any sexual activity (WHO prioritises girls aged 9–14) but adults can discuss catch-up vaccination with a doctor. India has an indigenous HPV vaccine. Vaccinated women still need cervical screening.

activity.prompt: Questions people are too shy to ask at an STI clinic

items.a: No. Testing is confidential; results are given to you.

items.q: Do I have to describe what I did?
items.a: Only what's needed to choose the right tests — staff hear this every day and won't judge.

items.q: I'm married. Can I still get an STI?
items.a: Yes. Marital status doesn't protect anyone; testing before or within a relationship is responsible.
Usually brief discomfort, not pain. Tell the clinician if you are anxious — they can go slowly.

quiz.q: Within how many hours must HIV PEP be started?
quiz.why: Sooner is better; 72 hours is the outer limit.

quiz.q: India's National AIDS helpline number?
Best age group for HPV vaccine per WHO priority?
After HPV vaccination, cervical screening is…
quiz.why: Vaccines don't cover every high-risk type.

scenes.text: Your friend Isha calls: 'We didn't use anything last night. I'm panicking.'
You stay calm and help her think step by step.

steps.title: Steps that matter
steps.body: 1) Emergency contraception as soon as possible. 2) Think about STI risk and testing. 3) If HIV exposure is possible, go for PEP within 72 hours. 4) Plan regular contraception.

steps.title: Tone
steps.body: No blame. 'Thanks for telling me. Let's sort this out' works far better than 'How could you?'

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body: Work through the activity below. There is no single perfect script — aim for responses that are accurate, kind and respectful of everyone's choices. Afterwards, note one thing you would say differently in real life.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body:
- **112** — any emergency
- **Tele-MANAS 14416** — free 24×7 mental health support
- A registered doctor, gynaecologist, urologist, psychiatrist or counsellor for anything personal

This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

a.text: Isha says: 'Should I just wait and see?' What do you say?

choices.label: Encourage EC from a pharmacy today — sooner works better
choices.feedback: Correct priority.

choices.label: Yes, wait for your period
choices.feedback: Waiting reduces EC effectiveness.

choices.label: Tell her to douche
choices.feedback: Douching doesn't prevent pregnancy or STIs and can cause infection.

b.text: She mentions her partner's HIV status is unknown and he had other partners. Next?

choices.label: Suggest she ask a hospital or ART centre about PEP today, then STI testing later
choices.feedback: PEP is time-critical.

choices.label: It's fine, she looks healthy
choices.feedback: Looks tell you nothing.

end.text: Isha gets EC, is assessed for PEP and books a test. She's relieved — and starts a regular method.

courses.title: Safer sex & consent in long relationships and marriage
courses.summary: Consent doesn't stop after the wedding. Learn ongoing consent, talking about desire and boundaries, safer-sex habits across a relationship, and what the law says in general terms.
outcomes: Explain ongoing, revocable consent in committed relationships
Use scripts for talking about sex and boundaries
Plan safer-sex habits including testing and condoms
Recognise coercion within relationships
courses.guardianNote: Adults-only (18+) course: medically accurate, non-explicit and judgment-free health education.

lessons.title: Consent is ongoing — even after 10 years

scenes.text: Anil assumes 'we're married, so yes is always yes'.
Poonam often feels too tired but says nothing.
A counsellor helps them talk about it openly.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What consent means
steps.body: Consent is **freely given, informed, enthusiastic, specific and reversible**. It is given each time, can be withdrawn at any moment, and saying yes to one thing is not yes to everything.

steps.title: Silence is not consent
steps.body: Being tired, asleep, drunk or quietly going along to avoid a fight is not freely given consent. Check in: 'Are you up for this?' 'Want to stop?'

steps.title: Coercion
steps.body: Pressure, guilt-tripping, threats, sulking until someone gives in, or making them 'owe' you are forms of coercion — they harm trust and wellbeing.

steps.title: Law in general terms
steps.body: Indian law criminalises sexual assault and provides protection from domestic violence (Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005). The legal position on marital rape is under judicial consideration — but ethically and for health, consent matters in every relationship. This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: Being married means consent is permanent.
statements.why: Consent is given each time and can be withdrawn.

statements.s: Someone can change their mind midway.
statements.why: Consent is reversible.

statements.s: Sulking until a partner agrees is a form of pressure.
statements.why: Coercion isn't only force.

statements.s: Checking in kills romance.
statements.why: Most couples find it builds trust and closeness.

quiz.q: Consent must be…
Which is NOT consent?
Guilt-tripping a partner into sex is…
Which act protects women from domestic violence?
quiz.why: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

lessons.title: Talking about desire, no's and differences

scenes.text: Imran wants intimacy more often than Zoya.
Both feel rejected or pressured.
They learn a weekly 10-minute 'check-in'.

steps.title: Mismatched desire is common
steps.body: Almost every long-term couple has periods where one partner wants sex more. It isn't a sign of a failed relationship.

steps.title: Scripts that help
steps.body:
- 'I love being close to you. Can we talk about what we each enjoy?'
- 'Not tonight — but I'd love a cuddle.' (a no to sex, a yes to closeness)
- 'What would make it easier for you to feel in the mood?'

steps.title: Rules of the talk
steps.body: Pick a calm time, not in bed right after a rejection. Use 'I' statements. Listen without arguing. Agree on one small experiment.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If talking keeps turning into fights, a couples counsellor or sex therapist can help. Sudden changes in desire can have medical causes worth checking.

activity.prompt: Write one sentence you could use to start a calm conversation with a partner about intimacy or boundaries.
activity.hint: Start with appreciation, use 'I', and ask a question.

quiz.q: Desire mismatch in long relationships is…
A good time to talk about sex is…
'Not tonight, but I'd love a cuddle' shows…
options: A no to sex while keeping closeness
quiz.why: Separates the act from the relationship.

quiz.q: Who can help if talks keep failing?

scenes.text: Deepa and Karan are getting married and want to stop using condoms.
Their doctor suggests both get tested first.
They choose a new method together.

steps.title: Before stopping condoms
steps.body: Both partners test for STIs including HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, agree on exclusivity honestly, and choose another contraceptive if pregnancy isn't wanted.

steps.title: Other habits
steps.body: Use water- or silicone-based lubricant with latex condoms (oil-based products like coconut oil or petroleum jelly weaken latex). Use a new condom each time. Hepatitis B vaccination is worth asking about.

steps.title: Reducing risk
steps.body: Condoms, HPV and hepatitis B vaccines, regular testing, PrEP where appropriate, and treating infections promptly together reduce STI risk a great deal.

scenes.text: Suresh, 48, has had trouble keeping an erection for months and feels ashamed.
He nearly buys a 'herbal power' remedy advertised on TV.
His GP finds high blood sugar and blood pressure instead.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Very common
steps.body: Erectile dysfunction (ED) becomes more common with age, and occasional difficulty happens to almost everyone. Persistent ED deserves a check-up.

steps.title: ED can be an early warning
steps.body: ED often comes from reduced blood flow — the same process behind heart disease. Diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, heavy drinking, some medicines, low testosterone, depression and stress are common causes.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Treating the cause, lifestyle change, counselling, and prescribed medicines (PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil or tadalafil). These must be prescribed: they are **dangerous with nitrate heart medicines**.

steps.title: Early (premature) ejaculation
steps.body: Very common, especially with anxiety or new partners. Behavioural techniques, counselling, and sometimes prescribed medicines help. It is not a disease of 'weakness'.

steps.title: Avoid quacks
steps.body: Unlabelled 'power' capsules may contain hidden prescription drugs or heavy metals. See a registered doctor, urologist or andrologist.

statements.s: ED can be an early sign of heart disease.
statements.why: Blood vessels in the penis are small and show problems early.

statements.s: ED medicines are safe with nitrate heart pills.
statements.why: The combination can drop blood pressure dangerously.

statements.s: Occasional erection problems are normal.
statements.why: Stress, tiredness and alcohol affect everyone sometimes.

statements.s: Herbal 'power' remedies sold on TV are always safe.
statements.why: Some contain hidden drugs.

scenes.text: Anjali, 38, mother of two, says she 'just doesn't feel like it anymore'.
She worries something is wrong with her — or her marriage.
Her doctor checks thyroid, iron, medicines and mood, and asks about sleep and stress.

steps.title: Desire changes
steps.body: Desire naturally rises and falls with stress, sleep, parenting, illness, relationship conflict, hormones and age. Many people feel 'responsive desire' — interest grows after closeness starts — rather than spontaneous desire.

steps.title: Possible medical contributors
steps.body: Depression and some antidepressants, thyroid problems, anaemia, low testosterone, hormonal contraception in some people, breastfeeding, menopause, chronic pain, alcohol.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body: Treat causes, share household load, protect sleep, plan unhurried time together, communicate, and consider a sex therapist. Low desire is only a 'problem' if it bothers you.

items.q: Is it normal not to want sex for months?
items.a: It can be, especially during stress, illness or with young children. It's worth exploring if it bothers you or your partner.
Yes, some can. Don't stop them suddenly — talk to your doctor, who may adjust the treatment.
No. Asexuality is an orientation — some people experience little or no sexual attraction and are not ill.
No. It helps only when levels are truly low and should only be prescribed after proper tests.

options: Desire that appears after closeness begins

scenes.text: Shreya, married eight months, finds penetration very painful and feels she's failing.
Relatives keep asking about 'good news'.
A gynaecologist explains vaginismus and refers her to a pelvic-floor physiotherapist.

steps.title: Pain is a signal, not a duty
steps.body: Pain with sex (dyspareunia) is common and should never be 'pushed through'. Causes include dryness, infections, endometriosis, skin conditions, scarring after childbirth, menopause changes, and **vaginismus** — involuntary tightening of pelvic muscles, often linked with fear or anxiety.

steps.title: Treatment works
steps.body: Depending on cause: treating infections, lubricants or vaginal moisturisers, local oestrogen after menopause, pelvic-floor physiotherapy, graded dilator therapy, counselling or sex therapy. Most people with vaginismus improve with treatment.

steps.title: Men can have pain too
steps.body: Pain in men can come from infections, tight foreskin (phimosis), Peyronie's disease (curvature) or prostatitis — a urologist can help.

steps.title: Partners
steps.body: Stop if it hurts, take penetration off the table for a while if advised, and focus on other kinds of closeness while treatment works.

statements.s: Pain with sex should be endured.
statements.why: Pain is a signal to stop and seek care.

statements.s: Vaginismus is treatable.
statements.why: Physiotherapy, dilators and counselling help most people.

statements.s: Endometriosis can cause pain with sex.
statements.why: Deep pain is a common symptom.

statements.s: Only women can have pain during sex.
statements.why: Men can too.

steps.title: What partners can do
steps.body: Respond with warmth, not blame. Go to appointments together if wanted. Remember intimacy is wider than intercourse.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Jokes about 'manhood', suspicion of affairs, or pressure to 'perform'.

courses.title: First-time myths, sex after childbirth & sex after 50
courses.summary: Clears up harmful myths about virginity and the 'first night', explains how bodies and intimacy change after childbirth, and how sexual health continues into later life.
outcomes: Debunk hymen and 'first-night' myths
Describe physical and emotional recovery after childbirth
Explain sexual health changes after 50 and how to manage them
Remember that STI protection matters at every age
courses.guardianNote: Adults-only (18+) course: medically accurate, non-explicit and judgment-free health education.

scenes.text: Before her wedding, Kavya hears that she 'must bleed' on the first night.
Her fiancé Varun has heard he must 'perform' perfectly.
They read accurate information together.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: The hymen myth
steps.body: The hymen is a thin, flexible tissue that varies naturally; many women do not bleed the first time. Its appearance cannot prove whether someone has had sex.

steps.title: 'Virginity tests' are unscientific
steps.body: WHO and UN agencies have called 'virginity testing' unscientific and a human-rights violation. India's Supreme Court has condemned the 'two-finger test' and said those conducting it may be held guilty of misconduct.

steps.title: The first time
steps.body: It's normal to feel nervous. Go slowly, use lubricant, communicate, and stop if it hurts. It is not a performance; many couples take days or weeks to feel comfortable.

steps.title: Pregnancy and STIs
steps.body: Pregnancy and STIs are possible the first time — plan contraception before the wedding.

statements.s: Bleeding proves first-time sex.
statements.why: Many people don't bleed; bleeding can have other causes.

statements.s: 'Virginity tests' are scientifically valid.
statements.why: They are unscientific and condemned.

statements.s: Pregnancy can happen the first time.
statements.why: No exemption exists.

statements.s: Taking time to become comfortable is normal.
statements.why: There's no deadline.

scenes.text: Pooja had a baby 6 weeks ago; her husband asks when they can be intimate again.
She is exhausted, sore and breastfeeding.
At her postnatal check the doctor talks through recovery.

steps.title: Recovery takes time
steps.body: Many doctors suggest waiting until bleeding has stopped and the postnatal check (around 6 weeks), but readiness is personal — some take months. Stitches, caesarean wounds, tiredness and emotions all matter.

steps.title: Breastfeeding and dryness
steps.body: Breastfeeding lowers oestrogen, which can cause vaginal dryness. Lubricant helps. Breastfeeding also lowers desire for many people — this is normal.

steps.title: Fertility returns
steps.body: You can ovulate before your first period returns. Exclusive breastfeeding only works as contraception under strict conditions (baby under 6 months, fully breastfed, no periods) — plan a method.

steps.title: Pelvic floor
steps.body: Pelvic-floor exercises help bladder control and comfort. Persistent pain, leakage or low mood are reasons to see a doctor.

items.q: Is it normal not to want sex after a baby?
items.a: Very. Exhaustion, hormones and body changes are common reasons. Closeness can be rebuilt gradually.
It may feel different at first. Go slowly, use lubricant, and see a doctor if pain persists.

items.q: Can I get pregnant while breastfeeding?
items.a: Yes, unless strict conditions are met. Use contraception if you don't want another pregnancy soon.

items.q: What if I feel sad all the time?
items.a: That may be postpartum depression — speak to a doctor. Tele-MANAS 14416 can help.

scenes.text: Kamala, 58, and her husband are recently retired and want to rekindle intimacy.
They notice dryness for her and slower erections for him.
Their doctor reassures them these changes are common and manageable.

steps.title: Desire doesn't retire
steps.body: Many people remain sexually interested and active into their 70s and beyond. Intimacy can become more relaxed and less goal-focused.

steps.title: Common changes
steps.body: After menopause: dryness and thinning of vaginal tissue (genitourinary syndrome of menopause) — treatable with moisturisers, lubricants or local oestrogen. Men: slower arousal, softer erections — often linked to vascular health and medicines.

steps.title: STIs don't stop at 50
steps.body: Older adults who start new relationships should still use condoms and test — STI rates in older adults have been rising in several countries.

steps.title: Medicines and conditions
steps.body: Diabetes, heart disease, arthritis and blood-pressure tablets can affect sex — ask your doctor about adjustments rather than giving up.

statements.s: People lose all interest in sex after 50.
statements.why: Many remain interested lifelong.

statements.s: Vaginal dryness after menopause is treatable.
statements.why: Lubricants, moisturisers, local oestrogen.

statements.s: Older adults don't need condoms with new partners.
statements.why: STI risk exists at every age.

statements.s: Some blood-pressure medicines can affect erections.
statements.why: Your doctor may adjust them.
